title: How Samoan sounds
summary: You'll know the three kinds of Samoan (everyday, orator and polite) and the T and K styles of speech. You'll also hear how vowel length and the glottal stop change a word.

notes.point: Samoan has everyday language (gagana o aso uma), orator language used by matai in their meetings, and polite language (gagana faʻaaloalo) used about the person you speak to and their things.

There are two styles of speech. The T style (tautala saʻo) is used for writing, church, school and talking to foreigners. Most everyday talk is in the K style (tautala sesē), where t sounds like k and n like g.
Samoan was first written with five vowels and nine consonants. The letters k, r and h were borrowed later, mostly for words that came from outside.
A long vowel (with a macron) or a glottal stop (the ʻokina) can make a different word, so listen for them.
The verb usually comes first, before the subject.

words.en: chief; head of a Samoan family

phrases.sm: ʻIoe, ʻou te lē fia ʻai.
phrases.en: Yes (that's right), I don't want to eat.

practice.q: Which style is used for writing and church?
In the K style, what does Tālofa become?
Someone asks E te lē fia ʻai? and you don't want to eat. What do you say?
options: ʻIoe, ʻou te lē fia ʻai.
Leai, ʻou te lē fia ʻai.

culture: A negative question is answered by agreeing with it: to "Don't you want to eat?" ʻIoe (yes) means "Yes, I don't." People often say a lot with their eyes too.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 1

title: The sounds, up close
summary: Learn the Samoan letters, how a long vowel or an ʻokina can turn one word into another, how to say g, and which syllable to stress. Then practise saying common nouns for people, places and things.

notes.point: The alphabet is small: five vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and ten consonants, which are f, g, l, m and n, then p, s, t and v, plus the ʻokina (ʻ). Missionaries wrote the language down in the 1800s; h, k and r were added afterwards for words taken from other languages.

examples.en: coffee (borrowed, so it has a k)

notes.point: Compare tala and tālā: the only difference is the macron, and the meaning is completely different. Each of the five vowels comes in a short and a long version, and the macron (as in ā or ō) marks the long one.
The ʻokina is a letter in its own right. Say it as a quick stop of the breath, like the break in the middle of English "uh-oh". Drop it and you may be saying a different word.
Read every g as the ng in singer. It never sounds like the g in go. Most other consonants are close to their English sounds, and s is a little lighter.
When two vowels meet, say both of them. An i in front of another vowel slides toward the sound of English y, and a u slides toward English w, even though y and w are not Samoan letters.

Most words are stressed on the next to last syllable: PU-ta. If the last vowel is long, or the word finishes with two vowels together, the stress shifts to the end. The macron shows a long vowel, and a long vowel carries stress.
People speak in two styles. The T style is used in writing, on the radio, in church and in careful speech. The K style is relaxed everyday talk: t is said as k, n as g, and r as l.

practice.q: How is the g in 'gagana' said?
What is 'mother' in the casual K style?

culture: In many families the most valued gift is an ʻie tōga, a fine mat woven very tightly by hand. Families give these mats and accept them at weddings, at funerals and at other large events.
sources: Written for this project

title: Greetings
summary: You'll be able to say hello, ask how someone is and answer. You'll also know the everyday greeting questions like "Where are you going?" and how to answer them.

notes.point: Tālofa is used when you are first introduced to someone. Day to day, people greet with Mālō or Mālō le soifua.
To answer a greeting, add foʻi (also).
ʻO ā mai ʻoe? asks how someone is. Answer Manuia lava faʻafetai, then turn it back with ʻAe ā ʻoe?
Greeting questions like "Where are you going?" don't need an exact answer.

examples.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te alu i ai?
ʻOu te alu i laʻu feʻau.

notes.point: E is the present tense marker. Right after a pronoun it becomes te.

words.en: present tense marker after a pronoun

phrases.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te alu i ai?
ʻO fea sā ʻe i ai?
ʻOu te alu i laʻu feʻau.

lines.sm: Manuia lava faʻafetai. ʻAe ā ʻoe?
ʻO fea ʻe te alu i ai?

practice.q: What does Manuia lava faʻafetai mean?
Someone asks ʻO fea ʻe te alu i ai? What kind of answer do they expect?

culture: Greeting questions like "Where are you going?" or "Where have you been?" are just hello and don't need an exact answer. Greetings often carry a joke, and you can answer with one.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 2

title: More greetings
summary: Say hello and goodbye, tell people your name, and ask how someone and their family are. A few polite words for elders, ministers and chiefs, and the casual K style, are included too.

notes.point: One word, tālofa, covers hello at any hour of the day. Put lava after it to sound warmer and more polite.
Your name goes after ʻO aʻu ʻo. To ask for someone else's, say ʻO ai lou igoa? The reply can be just ʻO plus the name.
Follow ʻO ā mai with ʻoe, or with the person you are asking about, to ask how they are. Once you have answered, send the question back with ʻAe ā and the person.

examples.sm: Tālofa lava, Nana. ʻO ā mai ʻoe?
Manuia faʻafetai. ʻAe ā lau susuga?

notes.point: Manuia faʻafetai (fine, thanks) is the answer you will hear most. If the other person has already said it, put foʻi (also, too) in yours.

Faʻaaloalo is respect. When you speak with an elder, a minister, a chief or an orator, many ordinary words are replaced by polite ones. A few of them change again depending on whether you address a chief or an orator.

examples.en: welcome (to a chief) / welcome (to an orator)

notes.point: Samoan is written in the T style, but in daily conversation most people use the K style, where k replaces t and g replaces n.

examples.sm: Manuia lava faʻafetai. / Maguia lava faʻafekai.
examples.en: Fine, thank you (T style / K style).

phrases.note: Use this when someone asks about another person, such as your mother.
A longer, kinder way to say goodbye.
A polite greeting. The other person replies Mālō foʻi le soifua (good health to you too).
A respectful way to tell a guest or an older person to come in, in place of sau.

lines.sm: Tālofa lava. ʻO aʻu ʻo Sina.
Tālofa lava, Sina. ʻO aʻu ʻo Ioane.
Manuia foʻi faʻafetai. ʻO ā mai lou tinā?
lines.en: Fine too, thanks. How is your mother?

lines.sm: ʻOloʻo manuia faʻafetai. ʻAe ā lou tamā?
lines.en: She's fine, thanks. And your father?

practice.sm: Tālofa lava, Nana. ʻO ā ___ ʻoe?

practice.q: Which is the respect word for 'name'?
Someone greets you and asks how you are. What is a good answer?
How do you welcome a chief?
What is 'faʻafetai' in the casual K style?

culture: At a family gathering or a village meeting, people use polite words when they talk with elders, and special titles of honour for chiefs and orators. Knowing a handful of these, like susū mai and lau susuga, helps a visitor show respect.
sources: Written for this project
Some phrases: J. F. Mayer, Samoan Language (Peace Corps, 1975)

title: This, that and those
summary: You'll be able to say what something is and point to it as this, that or that over there. You'll also ask "What is this?" and "Is this a pen?"

notes.point: ʻO le names one thing; ʻo alone (no le) names more than one.
After the noun, lea means this (by me), lenā means that (by you) and lale means that over there.
For more than one, use ia (these), nā (those, by you) and lā (those over there).
Ask what something is with ʻO le ā, or ʻO ā for more than one.
In a yes or no question, le becomes se, and no article becomes ni.

phrases.en: Yes, that's a pen over there.

practice.q: ʻO le laulau lenā. What does it mean?
Which word means that over there?

sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 3

title: Pointing: this, that, these, those
summary: Point at things and name them, using three distances: close to you, close to the listener, and far from you both. Ask what one thing or several things are.

notes.point: Pick the word by distance. Near the speaker: lenei (or lea). Near the listener, or not far off: lenā (or lele). Far from both of you: lelā (or lale).

examples.en: That is the post office (over there).

notes.point: Talking about several things? Take the le off the front of the word: nei means these, nā means those by you, lā means those over there. Lea becomes ia.
The noun stays exactly the same in the plural. Only le disappears.
You may put the pointing word in front of the noun or behind it, with no change in meaning.
The question word is ā (what). For one thing ask ʻO le ā …?, for more than one ʻO ā …? Said by itself, ʻO le ā? is also the reply when someone calls your name, like English "What?"

examples.sm: ʻO le ā le mea lea?

notes.point: A question can open with po (or pē), but in speech it is often left off. Answer with ʻioe (yes) or leai (no).

examples.sm: Po ʻo le ā lelā mea?
Po ʻo lenā mea ʻo se uati?
examples.en: Is that thing a watch (by you)?

words.en: that (away from us both), other form

phrases.sm: ʻO le ā le mea lea?

phrases.en: What is that building over there?

lines.sm: ʻO le ā le mea lea?

lines.en: That's the post office, over there.

practice.q: Which means 'that (far away from both of us)'?
What is the plural of lenā?

options: ʻO le ā le mea lea?

culture: At many feasts the roast pig is the main dish. In a lot of villages it is the young men without titles (tāuleleʻa) who get the pig ready and bake it in the ʻumu, an oven of hot stones.
sources: Written for this project

title: A, the, some
summary: Use le where English says "the" and se where it says "a", and see how both change when there is more than one thing. A few words for people also change shape in the plural.

notes.point: Le is "the" and se is "a". When a noun stands alone, or opens the sentence, ʻo goes in front of it.
If the speaker means one particular person or thing, Samoan uses le, even in places where English would say "a".

examples.en: I am a Peace Corps Volunteer.

notes.point: Se is for any one out of many, in questions that ask if something is there or what it is, and after a negative.

examples.en: May I have a pen, please?

notes.point: For more than one: le simply drops away, and se is replaced by ni (some, any). In relaxed speech people often leave ni out as well.

examples.sm: ʻO se pasi. / ʻO ni pasi.
E iai ni tou pani, faʻamolemole?
examples.en: Do you have any buns, please?

notes.point: A Samoan noun normally looks the same for one or many. The exceptions are a small group of words for people, which grow or shrink in the plural.

examples.en: a man's sister / a man's sisters

words.en: marker before a noun or pronoun at the start

phrases.en: May I have a pen, please?

lines.en: Is that a chicken over there?

practice.q: What is the plural of 'ʻO se pasi'?
What is the plural of tamaitiiti (child)?

culture: A tauleʻaleʻa is a man who holds no chief's title. In many villages these young men belong to a group of their own, and that group takes on much of the hard physical work, such as getting food ready for a feast.
sources: Written for this project

title: Introducing yourself
summary: You'll be able to give your name, where you're from, your age, your job and whether you're married. You'll also ask other people the same.

notes.point: Igoa is the everyday word for name; suafa is the polite one. Use suafa when asking a respected person, but never for your own name.
You'll be asked your age a lot. Answer E, then the number, then oʻu tausaga.
There are two words for my. Loʻu is for people and things close to you, like family; laʻu is for most other things. A wrong one is usually understood, but sometimes it changes the meaning.
A short answer starts with ʻo.

phrases.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai?

lines.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai?

practice.q: Which is the polite word for name?
What does ʻO fea ʻe te sau ai? ask?

culture: People often ask your age and whether you're married, and children love asking your name in English. Decide ahead how you want to answer.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 4

title: Starting with ʻo
summary: There is no Samoan word for is, am or are. Put ʻo at the front and a noun becomes a full sentence, such as "It's a dog". This lesson also covers ʻo with question words, and the places a subject takes ʻo and the places it does not.

notes.point: ʻO in front of a noun or a name gives you a whole sentence. In English you would add it is or they are.
Compare le nofoa with ʻO le nofoa. The first is only a name for a thing, the chair. With ʻo in front it says something: it's the chair.
You can add a describing word or a pointing word (lenei, lenā, lale) after the noun and keep ʻo at the front.
Question words (ai, fea, ā), pointing words and se isi take ʻo too, when they start the sentence or are said alone.
Word order decides whether the subject takes ʻo. At the front it does. After the verb it does not. Both sentences below mean the same thing.
Ia (he, she, it) breaks that rule: it keeps ʻo wherever it goes, also after the verb.

words.en: it is, they are (starts a statement)

phrases.note: A short answer starts with ʻo.

lines.sm: ʻO Ioane. Sā tamoʻe ʻo ia.

practice.q: Which means 'The boy ran' with the verb first?
What does ʻO ā nā mea? mean?

sources: Written for this project

title: Numbers and counting
summary: You'll be able to count from one to a thousand and ask how many things or people there are. You'll also meet the special counting words used when food and gifts are announced.

notes.point: Tens are built by putting a number before sefulu; ma le joins hundreds to the rest.
E fia asks how many things; E toʻafia asks how many people.
No verb for "there is" is needed: E and the number is enough.
People are counted with toʻa.

practice.q: Which means a hundred and eight?
Which do you use to count people?

culture: Samoan has special counting words for taro, cooked fish, crabs, mats and people. When food or gifts are brought for guests or the pastor, someone often calls out what each family gave, in a loud voice, as a public thank-you.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 6

title: More numbers
summary: Every number in Samoan is made from fourteen words: zero to ten, plus hundred, thousand and million. Count past a thousand, say first, second and last, and say how many each person gets.

notes.point: For the teens, say ten, then ma le, then the extra number. People usually skip the ma le and just say ten and the extra number.
A tens word is a number joined to sefulu: tolu + sefulu is thirty. The ones come straight after it.
Selau (hundred) and afe (thousand) take a number in front of them the same way.
When you count things, the order is e, the number, the noun. To ask the number, put fia where the number goes. With one thing, say e tasi le and the noun.
When you count people, the number gets toʻa joined to its front. The question word becomes toʻafia.
Muamua means first and mulimuli means last. For second, third and so on, say lona and the number.
Taʻi in front of the number means that many each. For people it is taʻitoʻa.

words.en: joined to a number when counting people

phrases.note: For things.
For people.

lines.sm: E toʻafia tamaiti i le potu?
lines.en: How many children are in the room?

sources: Written for this project

title: Yes, no and not
summary: Answer a question with ʻIoe (yes) or Leai (no), tell someone a thing isn't a shop or isn't a pencil, and use lē (not) before an action word or a describing word.

notes.point: Leai is no. ʻIoe is yes, and in relaxed talk it often shrinks to ʻī. To agree in a more formal, respectful way, say ʻO lea lava, meaning that is so.

examples.sm: ʻE te fia inu? Leai faʻafetai.
examples.en: Would you like a drink? No thank you.

notes.point: To say what something is not: E lē ʻo se + the noun. Here e is the present marker and lē means not; se (a) is used for one thing.

examples.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo se falemeli.
examples.en: No, it's not a post office.

notes.point: With several things, ni takes the place of se. When the answer is yes, there is no article at all, as with any plural.

examples.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo ni penitala nā.

notes.point: Lē also stands straight in front of the word it cancels, whether that is a verb (an action) or a describing word.

lines.en: Is that a bus over there?

lines.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo se pasi. ʻO le taʻavale.
lines.en: No, it's not a bus. It's a car.
Is that a hospital over there?

lines.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo se falemaʻi. ʻO le faleāʻoga.
lines.en: No, it's not a hospital. It's the school.

practice.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo se tamāloa.
Leai, e lē ʻo ni vaʻalele nā.

options: E lē ʻo le uati lenei.

practice.q: Make 'ʻIoe, ʻo le pusi lea' negative.
options: Leai, e lē ʻo se pusi lea.
Leai, e lē ʻo ni pusi.

practice.q: Where does lē go with a verb?
options: at the end of the sentence

practice.q: Which is a more formal way to agree?

culture: People often say yes without a word: they raise their eyebrows, sometimes with a small upward tilt of the head. If you ask a question and see this, the answer is yes.
sources: Written for this project

title: Review: this, that and the articles
summary: Practice with words you already know: this and that at three distances, their plural forms, and le, se and ni. Nothing new to learn here, only putting the pieces together.

notes.point: Pick the word by where the thing is. Close to the speaker: lenei or lea. Close to the listener: lenā. Away from you both: lelā or lale.
For several things, take the le off the front: lenei becomes nei (ia is also used), lenā becomes nā, lelā becomes lā.
Compare ʻO le ā …? (what is it, one thing) with ʻO ā …? (what are they, several things).
Le (the) and se (a) sit in front of the noun. Join nouns with ma (and). In the plural, every le goes away, and se turns into ni.

examples.sm: ʻO le fale ma le taʻavale. / ʻO fale ma taʻavale.
examples.en: The house and the car. / Houses and cars.

examples.sm: ʻO le peni ma le pepa. / ʻO peni ma pepa.
examples.en: The pen and the paper. / Pens and papers.

lines.en: Thanks. What are those over there?

practice.q: What is the plural of 'ʻO le mōlī ma le fale'?
options: ʻO ni mōlī ma le fale.

practice.q: What is the plural of 'ʻO lenā mea'?

sources: Written for this project

title: Family
summary: You can ask someone about their parents, brothers and sisters, and children, and answer the same questions about your own family. You can count people with toʻa and say who is the eldest or youngest.

notes.point: Uso is a brother or sister of the same sex as you: a man's brother, a woman's sister. A woman calls her brother tuagane; a man calls his sister tuafafine.

examples.en: I have two brothers (said by a woman).

notes.point: Lou (your) and loʻu (my) go with one person or thing; ou and oʻu go with more than one.
When you count people, put toʻa in front of the number. Ask how many people with E toʻafia? For things, use the plain number.
ʻO starts many sentences and questions, marking the topic.
ʻO loʻo shows something going on right now.

words.en: brother of a man, sister of a woman

phrases.sm: ʻO ai le igoa o lou tinā?

phrases.en: How many brothers (or sisters) do you have?
How many children do you have?

phrases.sm: ʻO ai le tamā o le ʻāiga?
phrases.en: Who is the father of the family?

phrases.sm: ʻO Sina le āvā a Siaki.
ʻO lātou ʻo le fānau a Site ma Meipo.
phrases.en: They are the children of Site and Meipo.

phrases.sm: ʻO ai le matai o le ʻāiga?
phrases.en: Who is the matai of the family?

phrases.sm: ʻO ai le igoa o lou toʻalua?

lines.en: How many sisters do you have?

lines.sm: E toʻatasi loʻu uso. E toʻalua oʻu tuagane.
lines.en: I have one sister. I have two brothers.

practice.en: How many brothers do you have?
How many children do you have?

practice.q: A woman talks about her brother. Which word does she use?
Which is right for counting people?

culture: A matai, a chief (aliʻi) or an orator (tulāfale), looks after a family's land and people; family members serve the matai and are looked after in turn. A saying sums it up: ʻO le ala i le pule ʻo le tautua, service is the way to authority.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 14

title: Describing words
summary: In Samoan the noun comes first and the describing word follows it: fale tele is a big house. Many describing words also have a plural form for plural nouns. Use them to talk about a person, an object or a city, and to say what is in a place.

notes.point: Name the thing, then describe it. The describing word goes straight after the noun.
A second noun placed after the first one describes it in the same way.
To say what a place or person is like, use this frame: ʻO, the name, then ʻo se, a noun and the describing word.

examples.sm: ʻO ʻAukilani ʻo se ʻaʻai tele.
ʻO ʻUpolu ʻo se motu mānaia.

notes.point: Singular and plural are marked on the describing word too. When the noun is plural (no le in front), switch to the plural form. Often a syllable is repeated (poto, popoto), though some change in other ways (laʻitiiti, lāiti).

examples.sm: ʻO le teine poto. / ʻO teine popoto.
ʻO le tusi laʻitiiti. / ʻO tusi lāiti.

notes.point: To say that something is in a place, or that a place has something, use E iai, then the thing, then i and the place.

examples.sm: E iai ʻaʻai tetele i Amerika.
examples.en: There are big cities in America.

examples.sm: E iai ʻAukilani i Niu Sila.

notes.point: Point at a place on a map or in a photo and ask ʻO fea …? The reply is ʻO and the place name.

phrases.note: Add lenā or lenei while pointing at a map or photo: ʻO fea lenā?

lines.sm: ʻIoe. E iai fale tetele i ʻAukilani.
lines.en: Yes. There are big buildings in Auckland.

lines.sm: ʻO Apia. ʻO Apia ʻo le laumua o Sāmoa.
lines.en: It's Apia. Apia is the capital of Sāmoa.

lines.sm: Leai, e lē ʻo se ʻaʻai tele. ʻO se ʻaʻai mānaia.
lines.en: No, it's not a big city. It's a lovely city.

practice.sm: ʻO Sini ʻo se ʻaʻai mānaia.

practice.en: There are big buildings in Apia.
practice.sm: E iai fale tetele i Apia.

practice.q: Where does a Samoan describing word go?
Which is the plural of laʻitiiti (small)?

culture: Apia, the capital, is on the north coast of ʻUpolu. Many families have relatives living in Auckland, Sydney or Los Angeles, so these city names come up in everyday conversation.
sources: Written for this project

title: Small talk: feelings, family and food
summary: You'll be able to say how you feel, talk about your host family and say what you ate or did. You'll also answer the friendly questions people often ask.

notes.point: Feoloolo means so so; mālosi means well and strong; faʻamaʻimaʻi means a bit sick.
E ā asks how something is and goes with nouns. Faʻapēfea works with nouns too, and it is the only one that goes with a verb.

examples.sm: E faʻapēfea ona fai le meaʻai?
examples.en: How do you make the food?

notes.point: Toʻa goes before numbers and words of amount when you count people.

examples.en: There are a lot of people.
There are only a few people.
There are 25 new Peace Corps volunteers.

notes.point: Lava adds emphasis: very, really.
Sā marks the past.

examples.sm: ʻO ā au mea sā fai ananafi?

words.en: chief; head of a Samoan family

phrases.sm: E te fiafia i lou ʻāiga?
phrases.en: Are you happy with your family?
There are a lot of people.

phrases.sm: ʻO ā au mea sā fai ananafi?

practice.en: There are a lot of people.

practice.sm: ʻO ā au mea sā fai ananafi?

practice.en: The chop suey was too salty.

practice.q: What is the opposite of toʻatele?
What is the opposite of fiafia?
Which can you use with a verb?

culture: Asking questions, some personal, is a common way to be friendly, and family and food come up most. When someone asks if your family is big, say how many there are and name some of them.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 5

title: Commands and warnings
summary: You'll be able to tell someone to do something or to stop, and to warn them to be careful. You'll also pass on what someone else said to do.

notes.point: A command is just the verb first, no subject.
ʻAua le means don't. Tāofi, tuʻu and soia all mean stop.
Faʻaeteete means be careful. Vaʻai neʻi warns of what might happen.
To pass on what someone said, use Na fai mai.

title: Telling someone what to do
summary: Give an instruction with a verb alone, or name the object and the place it should end up. Also: the short linking words (to, for, from, with) and place words such as luga (on) and lalo (under).

notes.point: A verb by itself is already a command. Add a place word to say where.
The thing being acted on comes straight after the verb. Watch the direction: ʻave moves something away from you (take), ʻaumai moves it toward you (bring).
I (sometimes spelled ʻi) covers to, at and in. Use iā instead when the next word is a name, a pronoun (me, him, them) or a month.
Four more linking words: for is mō or mā, with is ma, by is e, and from is mai.
For position words, build the phrase in three parts: i, the place word (luga, lalo, totonu, tua, tafatafa), then o and the thing.

examples.sm: Tuʻu le pūlou i luga o le fata.
examples.en: Put the hat on the shelf.

examples.sm: Tuʻu le polo i lalo o le laulau.
examples.en: Put the ball under the table.

notes.point: To pick out who must do the job, begin with that person's name. Faʻamolemole (please) at the end makes it polite.

phrases.sm: Tū i tafatafa o le faitotoʻa.

phrases.note: Put it at the end of a command to make it a polite request.

title: Telling time
summary: You'll be able to ask and say the time, from the hour to quarter past and five to. You'll also learn how time was told by the sun and the roosters.

notes.point: ʻUa tā le fia? (lit. it has struck how many?) asks the time. Answer ʻUa tā le and the hour.
ʻAfa is half past. Minutes past use e teʻa ai; minutes to use toe ... i le.

ʻUa toe lima minute i le ono.

culture: Time was told by the sun in the day and by the roosters at night, and the traditional day begins at sunrise. When the sun rises before six, people say "ʻUa tuai le taimi" (the clock is slow); in May and June it's "ʻUa vave le taimi" (it's quick).

title: What time is it?
summary: Ask what time it is and give the answer: on the hour, so many minutes past or to the hour, half past, and a quarter past or to. The numbers you already know do most of the work, with a few new words such as mīnute, teʻa and toe.

notes.point: The usual question is ʻUa tā le fia? Word for word it asks how many the clock has struck. You can also ask ʻO le ā le taimi? (what is the time?).
For a time on the hour, answer with ʻUa tā le and the hour number.
For minutes after the hour, the order is ʻUa, how many minutes, the word mīnute, e teʻa ai le, and the hour. Leave out the minutes (ʻUa teʻa le ...) and it means a little after that hour.

examples.sm: ʻUa luasefulu mīnute e teʻa ai le valu.

notes.point: For minutes before the hour, toe (left) comes first: ʻUa toe, the minutes, mīnute i le, then the coming hour.

examples.sm: ʻUa toe sefulu mīnute i le iva.
ʻUa toe luasefulu lima mīnute i le tasi.

notes.point: For half past, use ʻafa: ʻUa ʻafa le and the hour. For a quarter, put kuata where the minutes go, in either the past pattern or the to pattern.

examples.sm: ʻUa kuata e teʻa ai le ono.
ʻUa toe kuata i le lua.

notes.point: When you say when something happens, drop ʻUa and start with ʻo le and the time.

examples.sm: ʻO le ʻafa o le fitu.

title: Days, months and dates
summary: Say the days of the week and the months, and ask what day or date it is. You'll also name holidays and ask about birthdays.

notes.point: The days start with Aso (day).
Ask the date with ʻo le aso fia; answer with the number and o and the month.

title: Days and months
summary: Name every day and month, and ask what day it is today. Then say which day it was yesterday or will be tomorrow, and which month it is now.

notes.point: The question for today is ʻO le ā le asō? The reply starts with ʻO le, then the name of the day.
One macron changes the word. Asō with a long final o is today; aso with a short o is day or date.
For a date, ask with aso fia (day how-many). Answer ʻO le aso, the number, then o and the month.

examples.sm: ʻO le aso fia le fono?
ʻO le aso iva o Me.

notes.point: Add ananafi (yesterday) or taeao (tomorrow) to move the question or the answer to another day. In the answer it goes last.
Days take ʻO le, but months drop the le and take ʻO on its own. Ask the month with ʻO le ā le māsina lenei?
Some of these names were borrowed from English, and you will see them spelled with l or with r. Both spellings are correct.

phrases.sm: ʻO le aso fia le fono?

phrases.note: Said back to someone who thanks you, or to mean it doesn't matter.

culture: Sā means sacred, so Aso Sā is the sacred day. In many families Sunday is kept for church and for time together, with a big shared meal once the morning service is over.

title: Weather and seasons
summary: Ask and say what the weather is like today, last night and this week. You'll also talk about Samoa's two seasons and the hurricane months.

notes.point: For the past, use na: na matagi (it was windy), na timu (it rained). Add tele for very.

examples.en: It was very windy last night.

notes.point: ʻUa describes how things are now: ʻua lagilelei le tau (the weather is fine).

examples.sm: ʻIoe, ʻua lelei lava le tau.
examples.en: Yes, the weather has been really good.

notes.point: To wonder or doubt, use faʻamata (do you think) and masalo (maybe).

examples.en: Do you think it will rain?

notes.point: tau means both weather and season.

examples.en: How many seasons are there in Samoa?

examples.sm: ʻO le tau vevela ma le tau susū.
examples.en: The hot season and the wet season.

Do you think it will rain?

phrases.en: The weather has been stormy this week.

title: Shopping
summary: You'll be able to ask for things at the village shop or market, ask the price and understand the answer. You'll also know the names of everyday goods and food.

title: At the shop and the market
summary: Ask a shopkeeper whether they have something, ask what it costs, and ask them to bring it to you. Also the names of common foods and household goods, and what to say when something is sold out.

notes.point: At a shop, ask E iai ni tou ... ? to find out if they have something. Tou is 'you' meaning the people who run the shop.

examples.sm: E fia le tau o le iʻa?
ʻO le ā le tau o le pata?
examples.en: What is the price of the butter?

notes.point: A price is E, then the number, then tālā (dollars) or sene (cents). To give a price per item or per kilo, add i le.

notes.point: ʻAumai means bring. Follow it with se for 'a' or 'one' to ask for a single item.
The shopkeeper may say there is a lot, that something is sold out, or that they have none.

title: Where things are
summary: You'll be able to say where something or someone is: inside, outside, on, under, beside or behind. You'll also ask who is somewhere and how many people are there.

notes.point: Place words follow i: i totonu (inside), i fafo (outside), i luga (on), i lalo (under). Add o and the thing for inside the box, on the table.

title: Where is it?
summary: Ask where a thing or a person is with ʻO fea?, ask who is somewhere with ʻO ai?, and answer with ʻo lā e plus a place word such as inside, on top of or behind.

notes.point: To ask where, start with ʻO fea and then name the thing (with le) or the person.
The answer starts ʻO lā e, then i and the place. Lā stands for whatever was just asked about, one thing or several. Said quickly, lā e sounds like one word: lāe.

examples.sm: ʻO lā e i totonu o le fale.
ʻO lā e i tua o le fale.
examples.en: It's at the back of the house.

notes.point: To say what is there, put the thing or the name between ʻO and lā e.

examples.sm: ʻO le tupe lā e i totonu o le ʻato.
examples.en: The money is in the bag.

examples.sm: ʻO Sione lā e i le faleʻoloa.

notes.point: Compare lā e with lenei e, lenā e and lea e. Lā does not point anywhere. Lenei e means here by me, lenā e means there by you, and lea e also points to a spot you can show.

examples.sm: ʻO le peni lenei e i luga o le laulau.
examples.en: The pen is here on the table.

examples.sm: ʻO le maile lenā e i fafo.
examples.en: The dog is outside, there by you.

notes.point: Put a verb after lenei e, lenā e or lea e and it tells what someone is doing right there.

examples.sm: ʻO lea e fai le meaʻai.
examples.en: I'm making the food right now.

notes.point: Put ai in place of the name to ask who: ʻO ai lā e and the place. The reply puts the name where ai was.

title: Question words
summary: You can ask where, when, how, what, how many, who and why, and answer each kind of question. You can also use the short tags often added to questions.

title: Personal pronouns
summary: You can say who people are with the right pronoun for one, two, or three or more people, including or leaving out the person you are talking to. You can ask and answer whether someone is a teacher, a doctor, and so on.

notes.point: Samoan has pronouns for one person, for two (dual), and for three or more (plural).

examples.sm: ʻO lāʻua ʻo Toma ma Mele.
ʻO lātou ʻo Sione, Simi ma Sina.
examples.en: They are Sione, Simi and Sina.

notes.point: There are two kinds of we. Tāʻua and tātou include the person you are talking to; māʻua and mātou leave them out.

examples.sm: ʻO tāʻua ʻo Sina ma Mele.
examples.en: We (you and I) are Sina and Mele.

examples.sm: ʻO māʻua ʻo Sione ma Toma.
examples.en: We (he and I, not you) are Sione and Toma.

notes.point: Say what someone is with ʻo and se (a) or le (the). Make it negative with e leʻo.

Leai, e leʻo aʻu ʻo se fōmaʻi.

title: I, you, we: the pronouns
summary: A Samoan pronoun tells you whether you mean one person, two, or three and more. Each 'we' also says whether the listener is part of the group.

notes.point: English you can mean one person or many. Samoan splits it three ways: ʻoe for one, ʻoulua for exactly two, ʻoutou for three or more. We and they split the same way, so count heads before you pick the word.

examples.sm: ʻO ʻoulua ʻo Malia ma Tavita.
examples.en: You two are Malia and Tavita.

examples.sm: ʻO ʻoutou ʻo Malia, Tavita ma Pita.
examples.en: You (three or more) are Malia, Tavita and Pita.

notes.point: Is the listener part of the 'we'? If yes, use tāʻua (two) or tātou (more). If no, use māʻua (two) or mātou (more).

examples.sm: Tā ō taeao i le tīfaga.
examples.en: Let's go to the movies tomorrow (you and me).

examples.sm: Mā te ō ma laʻu uō i Faleseʻela.
examples.en: My friend and I (not you) are going to Faleseʻela.

notes.point: Ia stands for he, she or it. The sentence alone does not tell you which.
Most pronouns also have a shorter form: aʻu / ʻou, ʻoe / ʻe, ia / na, tāʻua / tā, māʻua / mā, ʻoulua / lua, lāʻua / lā, ʻoutou / tou. Right after the particle ʻo, only the full form is used.
Where does the pronoun sit? The short form goes in front of the verb, or just after a tense marker. The full form goes after the verb. The meaning does not change.
For emphasis, the sentence can open by naming the person (ʻo + full pronoun), and the short form then comes back in front of the verb.

examples.sm: ʻO aʻu nei, ʻou te nofo i Apia.
examples.en: As for me, I live in Apia.

words.en: we two, he or she and I, not you (exclusive)
we, all of us including you (inclusive)

phrases.note: Full form aʻu after ʻo, then the name. Put your own name in place of Sione.

phrases.en: Let's go (you and me), it's going to rain.
phrases.note: Tā means just the two of you.

lines.sm: Tālofa lava. ʻO aʻu ʻo Sina. ʻO ai ʻoe?
lines.en: Hello. I am Sina. Who are you?

lines.sm: Leai. ʻO aʻu ʻo le fōmaʻi.

lines.en: Let's go to the shop, you and me.

Which means 'they' for three or more people?
Which pronoun means he, she or it?
You and two friends are all going. Which 'we' fits?
Which short form can follow ʻo?

title: Helping out at home
summary: Ask what someone is doing, say what you're doing, and offer to help. You'll also be able to take or turn down an offer of help and tell someone to go rest.

notes.point: To ask what someone is doing right now, people often say ʻO ā au mea o fai? Add nā for there, by you.

examples.sm: ʻO ā au mea o fai?
ʻO ā au mea nā e fai?

notes.point: In speech, lea, nā and lā can stand in for o loʻo (is doing). They come from the words for this, those and those over there.

examples.sm: ʻO lea e fai le meaʻai.
examples.en: I'm making the food right now.

notes.point: To turn down help kindly, say it's enough and send the person off to rest.

phrases.sm: ʻO ā au mea o fai?
ʻO ā au mea nā e fai?
ʻO lea e fai le meaʻai.
Leai se mea, na o le mālōlō.
ʻAumai se mea ʻou te fai.
E te manaʻo i se fesoasoani?

title: Rooms and buildings
summary: Put fale in front of another word and you get the name of a building: a bank, a church, a post office. Here are the rooms and parts of a home, plus two questions for house hunting: E iai ...? (is there one?) and E fia ...? (how many?).

notes.point: Most building names are fale plus a second word. Treat each one as a single word with its own meaning.
Rooms follow the same plan with potu (room) in front. The second word often says what happens in that room.
E iai se ...? asks about one thing: is there one, or do you have one? Switch se to ni when you mean more than one.
To answer yes, start with ʻIoe and repeat e iai. To answer no, a plain Leai is enough.
When you ask whether someone has something of their own, your is sou with some nouns and sau with others, the same split as lou and lau. Learn which one goes with each noun.

examples.sm: E iai sou ʻāiga i Apia?
examples.en: Do you have family in Apia?

notes.point: E fia ...? asks for a number. The reply is e followed by the number.

phrases.note: Asked of a group, such as the people running a shop.

lines.en: Ioane, have you got a house?
Has it got a big kitchen?

practice.q: Which room do you sleep in?

culture: The traditional falesāmoa has no walls: a ring of wooden posts holds up a round roof, so the house stays open to the air on every side. In many villages a family's falesāmoa stands next to a falepālagi with walls, doors and windows.

title: Food likes and dislikes
summary: You can ask what food someone likes and say what you like or don't like. You can give a reason with ʻauā (because) and name your favourite.

notes.point: Fiafia i means to like. Put lē in front of fiafia for not.

examples.sm: ʻOu te fiafia i le palusami.
ʻOu te lē fiafia i faʻausi.

notes.point: Fia before a verb means want to.

examples.sm: ʻOu te fia ʻai i le palusami.

notes.point: Ask why with ʻAiseā …? and ai after the verb. Answer with ʻauā (because).

examples.sm: ʻAiseā e te fiafia ai i palusami?
ʻOu te fiafia i palusami ʻauā e mānaia.
examples.en: I like palusami because it's delicious.

notes.point: ʻAe means but.

examples.sm: ʻOu te fiafia i palusami ʻae ʻou te lē fiafia i oka.
examples.en: I like palusami but I don't like raw fish.

ʻOu te fiafia i le palusami.
ʻO le ā le meaʻai e te fia ʻai ai?
phrases.en: What food do you want to eat?

phrases.en: I don't like palusami because it's too rich.

title: Doing words
summary: A Samoan verb never changes for time, but many verbs take a second form when two or more people do the action. Here are everyday verbs with those forms, the prefix faʻa-, and phrases for asking and offering at a meal.

notes.point: Compare these two: savali is the same word in both. Only the small word in front tells you when it happened (see the tenses lesson).
With one doer you use the plain verb; with several, many verbs switch to a longer form, often by repeating a syllable. No rule predicts it, so learn both forms together.
A handful of plural forms barely look like the singular. Alu (go) becomes ō, sau (come) becomes ō mai, and inu (drink) becomes feinu.

examples.en: We two are going to Apia.

notes.point: Other verbs have only one form, whether one person or a crowd does it.
Faʻa- at the front of a word can do several things: make someone or something do the action, turn a noun into a verb, count how many times, or mean done the way a group does it.
At the table, ask with pasi mai (pass it to me) or ʻaumai (bring it), name the thing, and finish with faʻamolemole.

words.en: like, be happy (same in the plural)

phrases.sm: E te manaʻo i se kofe?

lines.en: Thanks. The chop suey is very nice.

lines.en: Yes, please. Who is the cook?

title: Making plans with your family
summary: You can ask what someone is doing tomorrow and say what you plan to do, or that you don't know yet. You can tell your family you won't be home for a meal or the night, and say when you will be back.

notes.point: Masalo means maybe or probably.

examples.sm: Masalo ʻou te alu i le malae vaʻalele.
examples.en: Maybe I will go to the airport.

notes.point: Moe means sleep, and also spend the night. Iā before a name means at that person's place.

examples.en: I will spend the night in Apia.

notes.point: Many verbs change for more than one person: savali / sāvavali (walk), nofo / nonofo (stay), siva / sisiva (dance), moe / momoe (sleep), ʻai / ʻaʻai (eat), pese / pepese (sing), galue / gālulue (work).
For "I went with Sione", Samoan counts everyone who went and uses a dual pronoun: we two went, me and Sione.

phrases.sm: ʻO le ā lau mea e fai taeao?

phrases.en: Are you going to school tomorrow?
Are you going to work tomorrow?

title: Casual invitations
summary: You can invite someone in your family to go for a walk, to a dance or to the movies. You can accept, or turn the invitation down politely and say why.

notes.point: Tā is "we two, you and I", and ō is the plural of alu (go). Tā ō … means let's go and do something.
Simple commands and suggestions need no tense marker. In a question the marker te follows the pronoun.
To turn someone down, start with malie (sorry) or leai and give a reason.

Plural verbs for groups: alu / ō (go), sau / ōmai (come), siva / sisiva (dance), pese / pepese (sing), tamoʻe / tāmomoʻe (run), taʻalo / tāʻaʻalo (play), inu / feinu (drink), savali / sāvavali (walk).

title: Making plans
summary: Ask if someone is free, invite them along, and accept. You'll also be able to say no and give a reason.

notes.point: To ask if someone is free, use avanoa (free time) with a time word.
Faʻamalie atu (sorry) softens a no. Follow it with a reason.

examples.sm: Faʻamalie atu, ʻou te lē avanoa.
Faʻamalie atu, e fai laʻu āʻoga.

E te sau i loʻu Aso Fānau?

title: Past, present and future
summary: You'll be able to say that something will happen, has happened, is going on or happened before. You'll also ask and answer yes or no questions in each tense.

notes.point: A tense marker goes before the verb: ʻo le ā (will), ʻua (has, just now), ʻoloʻo (is still), sā (did), e (does).
Make a question by raising your voice; the words stay the same.
For not, lē goes before the verb; for not yet or didn't, leʻi.
With I, the pronoun ʻou comes after the marker. After ʻou, e becomes te.

examples.sm: ʻIoe, ʻo le ā ʻou savali.

notes.point: Many verbs have a plural form for more than one person.

phrases.sm: ʻIoe, ʻo le ā ʻou savali.
Na ʻe sau anafea i Sāmoa?
phrases.en: When did you come to Samoa?

phrases.sm: ʻO ā au mea sā fai?

practice.q: What is the plural of siva?
What is the plural of alu?
What does Na ʻe sau anafea i Sāmoa? ask?

title: Now, before and later
summary: The verb stays the same and a short word placed before it tells you when the action happens. With six of these markers (ʻoloʻo, ʻua, sā, na, ʻoleʻā, and e or te) you can talk about what someone usually does, is doing now, has already done, did before and is going to do.

notes.point: E marks what usually happens, and now and then the future. It is e when the person doing it comes after the verb, but te when a pronoun comes just before it.
In the te pattern the pronoun is first and te follows it. The pairs to know: na te (she or he), ʻou te (I), mātou te (us, but not you), ʻe te (you), lua te (the two of you), mā te (the two of us).

examples.sm: Mā te ō i le faleʻoloa.
examples.en: We two are going to the shop.

notes.point: Use ʻoloʻo when the action is happening at this moment.
ʻUa usually tells you something has already happened. Put it with a word for weather or the time of day, though, and it describes the way things are right now.
Both sā and na point to the past. Sā tends to set a scene of something going on; na reports one action that is over.
ʻOleʻā looks ahead to something that will happen. The Peace Corps lessons write the same marker as ʻo le ā.
You will not find one Samoan word for to be, or one for to have. Patterns such as E iai (from the house lesson) cover those meanings.

lines.sm: ʻIoe, ʻua alu Pita i le āʻoga.
lines.en: Yes, Pita has gone to school.

lines.sm: Leai. Sā moe le pepe, ʻae ʻua ala.
lines.en: No. The baby was sleeping, but has woken up.

lines.sm: ʻOleʻā ʻou alu i le faleʻoloa.
lines.en: I will go to the shop.

practice.q: Which marker means something is going on right now?
Which marker comes right after a pronoun like ʻou?
What does ʻUa tā le iva mean?
What does Na tagi le teine mean?

title: Putting verbs to work
summary: Use each tense marker in short everyday sentences: what someone does, did, or is going to do, and why. You also learn verbs for standing, refusing, signing, saying, wanting, answering and pointing something out.

notes.point: Compare these two: Mele works at the shop, I work at the shop. With a name or a noun, the sentence opens with e and the person comes later, after the verb. A pronoun works the other way: the short pronoun and te come first, then the verb.

examples.sm: E galue Mele i le faleʻoloa.
ʻOu te galue i le faleʻoloa.

notes.point: The markers ʻua, ʻoloʻo, na, sā and ʻoleʻā can have a short pronoun tucked in right after them, before the verb.

examples.sm: Sā mātou ʻaʻai i le Tusitala.
Sā ʻou alu i le faleʻoloa.

notes.point: If a group is doing the action, switch to the plural verb: siva becomes sisiva, moe becomes momoe.
In Tom wrote the letter, Tom acts on something. A doer like that can take e in front of the name.

examples.sm: Na tusia e Toma le tusi.

notes.point: Mai and atu after a verb give its direction. Mai points to the speaker (come here, said to us). Atu points out and away (going over there, saying it to someone).

examples.sm: Na fai mai le faiāʻoga e tapuni le faitotoʻa.
examples.en: The teacher said to close the door.

notes.point: To a person is iā when a name or a pronoun follows.

examples.sm: Na ʻou ʻave le peni iā Toma.
examples.en: I gave the pen to Toma.

lines.sm: Sina, na ʻe alu i le faleʻoloa ananafi?
lines.en: Sina, did you go to the shop yesterday?

lines.sm: ʻIoe, na ʻou alu ma Pita.

lines.en: No. It was an old bag.

lines.sm: ʻOu te manaʻo i se ʻato fou.
ʻIoe, ʻoleʻā ʻou toe alu taeao.
lines.en: Yes, I will go again tomorrow.

practice.sm: ʻOu te galue i le faleʻoloa.
ʻOu te manaʻo i se taʻavale ___.

practice.q: Which direction word means toward the speaker?

culture: In many families, the young men who do not hold a chief's title (tāuleleʻa) cook and do the heavy work for their relatives and their chiefs. That service is called tautua.

title: Didn’t, won’t, isn’t
summary: The word lē, placed just before the verb, makes a sentence negative. Two more forms cover special cases: lē ʻo when something is not happening right now, and leʻi when something did not happen.

notes.point: Keep the tense marker where it is and slip lē in between it and the verb.
A sentence that starts with e becomes e lē, then the verb.

examples.sm: E lē fiafia Sina i le timu.

notes.point: ʻOloʻo lē is possible, but for something not happening at this moment people far more often say e lē ʻo (also spelled e leʻo).
Na lē and sā lē both work for the past, but you will often hear leʻi instead, after e or te.

examples.sm: Leai, ʻou te leʻi alu i Apia.
examples.en: No, I didn't go to Apia.

notes.point: To deny who or what someone is, start with e lē ʻo (or e leʻo), add the full pronoun, and finish with ʻo plus the name or noun.

examples.sm: E lē ʻo ia ʻo Sione.
Leai, e leʻo aʻu ʻo se fōmaʻi.
examples.en: No, I am not a doctor.

phrases.sm: ʻOu te lē alu peʻā timu.
phrases.en: I won't go if it rains.

lines.sm: Leai, ʻua lē sau le pasi.
ʻOloʻo timu. ʻOu te lē fiafia i le timu.
lines.en: It's raining. I don't like the rain.

lines.sm: Na sau Ioane i le pasi ananafi?
lines.en: Did Ioane come on the bus yesterday?

practice.sm: ʻOu te leʻi alu i Apia.
E lē ʻo ʻai le maile.
E lē ʻo ia ʻo Sione.

title: On the road in the village
summary: You can greet someone you meet on the road, ask where they have been or are going, and say where you are headed. You can also ask when they will be back and wish them a good day.

notes.point: Fea means where. At the end of a question it takes i (i fea); at the start it takes ʻo (ʻO fea). Both questions below mean the same thing.

examples.sm: ʻO fea e te alu i ai?

notes.point: Sā marks the past. In everyday speech sā ʻou (I did) is often run together.

examples.sm: Sā ʻou alu i le faleʻoloa.

notes.point: Atu shows movement away from the speaker, toward the person you are talking to or somewhere else. Mai shows movement toward the speaker.
Ai follows the verb in a question that starts with a question word, standing for the place or time asked about.

examples.sm: ʻO fea e te nofo ai?
ʻO le ā le taimi ʻe te sau ai?
examples.en: What time are you coming back?

notes.point: ʻA faʻapēfea? is the everyday way to ask where someone is off to. A vague answer like iʻō (over there) is fine.

phrases.sm: ʻO fea sā ʻe i ai?
Sā ʻou alu i le faleʻoloa.
ʻOu te alu atu i laʻu feʻau.

phrases.en: What time are you coming back?

lines.en: Hi to you too. Where have you been?

title: Arriving home
summary: Greet someone coming home and answer their greeting. Ask and say how the day went and what you did, then excuse yourself to rest.

notes.point: Greetings are often questions that answer themselves, like ʻUa ʻe sau? (So you've come?). The answer is just yes.
Mālō le onosaʻi praises someone for their patience or hard work. Answer with mālō foʻi to return it.

examples.en: Well done for sticking with it.

notes.point: Tele (very) always comes after the word it describes, not before it as in English.

words.en: to finish school for the day

phrases.en: Well done for sticking with it.

phrases.sm: ʻO ā au mea sā fai?
ʻOu te alu ʻou te mālōlō.

title: Meeting people of rank
summary: You can welcome a pastor, a teacher, a high chief or an orator with the right respectful words, and answer when they welcome you. You can also take your leave politely.

notes.point: Each welcome word goes with its own term of address: susū with susuga (pastors, teachers, guests, and anyone whose rank you don't know), afio with afioga (high chiefs), maliu with tōfā (orators).
The answer to a welcome names the person and their spouse: faletua for the wife of a chief, pastor, teacher or guest; tausi for the wife of an orator.

examples.sm: ʻIa, lau susuga ma le faletua.
examples.en: And you, sir, and your wife.

examples.sm: ʻIa, lau tōfā ma le tausi.
examples.en: And you, orator, and your wife.

notes.point: Mālō le soifua always follows the formal greeting.
Ia after a command makes it warmer: do come, go on then. It is how you take your leave.

examples.en: Go on then (to a high chief).

words.en: welcome, come (respectful, to pastors, teachers, guests)

term of address for a high chief
term of address for an orator
wife of a pastor, teacher, high chief or guest

title: Pronouns in a sentence
summary: Say who is doing what with short pronouns plus te, full pronouns after ʻo, and plural verbs for groups. You can also ask who someone is, ask where people are going, and say let's go.

notes.point: The short pronoun goes first, then te, then the verb. For one person: ʻOu te (I), Na te (he, she), ʻE te (you). For two: Tā te, Lā te, Lua te, Mā te. For three or more: Tātou te, Lātou te, Tou te, Mātou te.

examples.en: We (all of us) live in America.

notes.point: For a negative, lē comes straight after te.

examples.sm: ʻOu te lē fiafia i faʻausi.

examples.en: We two (not you) are not going.

notes.point: Let's is tā (just the two of you) or tātou (the whole group) followed directly by the verb. Leave out te here.

examples.en: Let's go for a walk (you and me).
Let's break up for the day (all of us).

notes.point: When two or more people act, many verbs change shape: ʻai to ʻaʻai, alu to ō, savali to sāvavali, galue to gālulue, siva to sisiva, pese to pepese.
With a tense marker, the short pronoun goes after the marker and before the verb.

examples.sm: Sā mātou ʻaʻai i le Tusitala.
examples.en: We (not you) ate at the Tusitala.

notes.point: To say what someone is or does for work: ʻo + full pronoun, then ʻo + the noun. With the two-person and group pronouns, ʻi is often added after the first ʻo, as in ʻO ʻi mātou or ʻO ʻi lāʻua.
Where are you going? follows the frame ʻO fea + short pronoun + te ō ʻi ai? Use lua for two people and tou for a group.

examples.sm: ʻO fea tou te ō ʻi ai?
examples.en: Where are you (three or more) going?

phrases.note: Said to a group that includes the listener.

phrases.sm: ʻO fea ʻe te alu i ai?
phrases.note: For two people say lua te ō, for a group tou te ō.

lines.sm: Lua te ō i le āʻoga?
lines.en: Are you two going to school?

lines.sm: ʻIoe, mā te ō ʻi le āʻoga.
ʻO aʻu ʻo Pita. ʻO aʻu ʻo le faiāʻoga.
lines.en: I am Pita. I am the teacher.

lines.sm: ʻO aʻu ʻo Malia. ʻOu te nofo i ʻAukilani.
lines.en: I am Malia. I live in Auckland.

practice.en: Let's break up for the day (all of us).

ʻO fea sā ʻe i ai?

title: Whose is it? My, your, his and her
summary: Say who owns something and ask whether something is yours, his or hers, for one thing or several. You'll answer yes or no with ʻioe and leai, e leʻo.

notes.point: Each possessive has an a form and an o form. A-nouns (bags, books, money, friends) take laʻu, lau, lana; o-nouns (houses, clothes, family, body parts) take loʻu, lou, lona.
To ask, use the indefinite form: saʻu, sau, sana (a) or soʻu, sou, sona (o).
Say no with e leʻo and the indefinite form.
For more than one thing, drop the l: aʻu, au, ana and oʻu, ou, ona. To ask, put ni before them.

examples.sm: Leai, e leʻo ni ana ʻato.

words.en: any of my, is it my
any of your, is it your
brother (of a man), sister (of a woman)

phrases.sm: Leai, e leʻo ni au ʻato.

sources: Gagana Samoa mō Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 29

title: My, your, his: two kinds
summary: Show who owns something (my pen, her nose, our house), choosing between two sets of words by what is owned, and switching forms for one thing or several. The vocabulary is the parts of the body.

notes.point: Each possessive joins la or lo to a short pronoun. My is laʻu or loʻu, your is lau or lou, his or her is lana or lona, and the pattern goes on for the other persons, such as lo mā for 'our' (two people, not you).

examples.en: our house (the two of us, not you)

notes.point: The lo set (loʻu, lou, lona) goes with your family, your body, your feelings, your clothes, and your house, boat or land.
The la set (laʻu, lau, lana) goes with everyday possessions such as a pen or a key, and also with food, animals, work, and words or language.

A few words go against this: a spouse (husband or wife), children, a baby, a child of a woman, a beard and a plantation all take the la set. Picking the wrong set can give a different meaning, as with susu.
When the owned things are more than one, take off the first l. Loʻu turns into oʻu, laʻu into aʻu, lana into ana, and la mātou into a mātou.
To say 'a' or 'any' instead of 'the', swap the l for s: saʻu or soʻu, sau or sou, sana or sona. With more than one thing, use ni and leave the s off, as in ni ou or ni a mātou.

examples.en: Does he or she have a pen?

examples.sm: ʻUa iai ni a mātou peni?

phrases.sm: ʻO ai le igoa o lou tinā?
phrases.note: Mother is family, so it takes lou.

phrases.en: How many children do you have?
phrases.note: Children take lau, one of the exceptions.

culture: At an ʻava ceremony, the person serving names who each cup is for as it is handed out, using a possessive. Lau ʻava lenei means the cup in front of you is yours.

title: Maps and places
summary: Name the directions, continents, oceans and a few countries, and ask where a place is. You'll also say why a place is hot or cold.

summary: Describe people, places and things with adjectives after the noun. Ask what someone or something is like and answer.

notes.point: A whole phrase can describe a noun too.

title: More describing words
summary: Put colours, numbers and other describing words after the thing they describe, and use the plural forms some of them have. By the end you can count objects and people and name the colour of something.

notes.point: Compare one big house with several: the noun fale stays the same, but tele changes to tetele. Nouns hardly ever change for more than one; many describing words do, and they sit after the noun.
A number goes after the noun as well, and e comes just before it.
When the things counted are people, the number starts with toʻa.
A colour word also comes after the noun. The word lanu (colour) is the first part of several colour names, such as lanumoana (blue), lanumeamata (green), lanupīniki (pink) and lanumoli (orange).
Several colours change when they describe more than one thing: paʻepaʻe to papaʻe, uliuli to uli, ʻenaʻena to ʻeʻena. Mūmū does not change.
Move the colour or number to the front with e and it works as the verb of the sentence, so you get 'is yellow' or 'there are three'.

words.en: added to a number when counting people

title: Saying what something is
summary: English uses am, is, are, was and were where Samoan uses several different patterns. Say that something is there or not, say who or what a person is, and describe how something was or will be.

notes.point: Iai means 'there is' or 'there are' when a tense marker comes in front: e for now, sā or na for the past.
For 'there is no' or 'there are no', use e leai, then se for one thing or ni for more than one.
For a name, a job or an identity, set two phrases that each start with ʻo next to each other. No word for 'is' is needed.

examples.sm: ʻO lātou ʻo le fānau a Site ma Meipo.
examples.en: They are the children of Site and Meipo.

notes.point: A describing word becomes a verb when a tense marker goes before it. Sā gives 'was', ʻoleʻā gives 'will be'.
After ʻua or ʻoloʻo, the English translation needs am, is or are, even though Samoan has no separate word for it.
A noun with just ʻo in front means 'it's' or 'here is'.

words.en: to be, be there, be available

phrases.en: Do you have any candy? (Are there any candies?)

title: Saying what you have
summary: Samoan says 'I have a pen' as 'there is my pen', using e iai with a word for my, your or his. You will tell people what you own, say what someone lacks, and ask a friend whether they have an umbrella or a car.

notes.point: E iai means 'there is'. Put my, your or his/her after it, then the thing, and the sentence means someone has it.
In a question, 'your' changes to the s- form: sau or sou. Someone who answers yes switches back to the l- form: laʻu or loʻu.
For 'not have', swap e iai for e leai and keep the s- form: saʻu or soʻu (mine), sana or sona (his/hers).
Each of these words comes in an a-form (laʻu, lana, saʻu) and an o-form (loʻu, lona, soʻu). Here clothes, umbrellas, houses and boats go with o; cars, pens, bags, money and dogs go with a.
The first word sets the time. E iai is the plain present, ʻua iai means someone has it now, and sā iai or na iai means they had it.
Describing words such as colours and big come after the thing they describe.

title: Who did what: word order
summary: A Samoan sentence usually opens with the verb, and small marker words show the doer and the thing acted on. You will read and build the same sentence, such as 'The carpenter built the house', in four different orders.

notes.point: Start with the time word (sā, na, ʻua, ʻoloʻo), then the verb, then the doer, then the thing: verb + subject + object.

examples.sm: Na ʻai e le ʻisumu le meaʻai.
Sā moe le toeaʻina i le nofoa.
examples.en: The old man slept in the chair.

notes.point: If the verb acts on something, e goes in front of the doer. That e is what tells you who did it, so the thing can come before the doer and nothing changes: verb + object + subject.

examples.sm: Na fau le fale e le tufuga.

notes.point: Compare a verb of moving, like alu. Nothing is acted on, so there is no e; the place someone goes to takes ʻi or i.

examples.sm: Na alu le faiāʻoga ʻi le āʻoga.
examples.en: The teacher went to the school.

notes.point: To start with the doer, put ʻO in front of it and drop the e: subject + verb + object. The verb then often gets an ending: fai becomes faia, ʻai becomes ʻaia.

examples.sm: ʻO Pita na ʻaia le iʻa.

notes.point: To start with the thing, put ʻO in front of it instead. Here the doer still has its e: object + verb + subject.

examples.sm: ʻO le puaʻa lenā na fafaga e Ioane.
examples.en: That is the pig Ioane fed.

notes.point: Position alone won't tell you who did what. Read the markers: e sits before the doer, ʻi before where someone goes, and ʻO before the word moved to the front.

title: Joining sentences: because, when, if, but

title: Joining ideas: because, but, if, while
summary: Small joining words link two ideas in one sentence: because, but, if, while and when. You will give a reason, add a 'but', and say what will happen if it rains.

notes.point: For a reason that is a full sentence, use ʻauā, leaga or ina ʻua. For a reason that is just a noun, such as the bus or the meeting, use ʻona ʻo.

examples.sm: ʻUa tagi le pepe ʻauā ʻua fia ʻai.
examples.en: The baby is crying because it is hungry.

examples.sm: Sā tuai le faiāʻoga ʻona ʻo le pasi.
examples.en: The teacher was late because of the bus.

notes.point: ʻAe (or the short ʻa) is 'but'. Add peitaʻi, as ʻae peitaʻi, when the second part happens in spite of the first.

examples.sm: ʻOu te fiafia ʻi le kofe ʻae ʻou te lē fiafia ʻi le falaoa.
examples.en: I like coffee, but I don't like bread.

examples.sm: Na vaivai le tama ʻae peitaʻi sā ia pese pea.
examples.en: The boy was tired, but he kept on singing.

notes.point: There are three words for 'if'. Peʻā is for something that may well happen, peʻāfai looks ahead to the future, and pe ʻana looks back at what would have happened.

examples.sm: ʻOu te lē tamoʻe peʻā timu.

Ina ʻua also means 'when' for something in the past.

title: Invitations on the road
summary: Accept or politely turn down the invitations people call out as you walk past. Ask where someone is going and say where you're headed.

notes.point: Susū maia is a polite come in, used to invite someone to eat or rest.

examples.en: Come and have something to eat.

title: Dinner with your host family
summary: You can offer to say grace, ask what a dish is and what it is made of, and accept or turn down more food. You can say you are full and thank the family for the meal.

notes.point: Seʻi means let: use it to suggest doing something now.
Toe means again or more. Offer more with toe and a verb of giving or serving.

examples.en: Shall I give you more soup?

notes.point: To accept, say faʻamolemole (please). Faʻafetai on its own can be taken as "no, thank you".
Māʻona means full; laulelei is the polite word.

title: Presenting a gift
summary: Give a short speech when you bring an oso (a food gift) to your Samoan family, and thank them when you leave. You'll also answer when they thank you.

notes.point: A gift speech starts by thanking God, then names the gift as small and humble with si (little, dear) and faʻatauvaʻa.

notes.point: End with a blessing: ia manuia.
A farewell thanks the family for their love and kindness and asks forgiveness for any wrong.

title: Answering rude words
summary: Tell someone to watch their language, and answer rude words with common comebacks. Most of them point the speaker back to how they were raised.

notes.point: Sōia means stop it. Put it in front to tell someone not to do something.
Many replies are sarcastic, praising the speaker's parents or upbringing to shame them.

examples.sm: E lē faʻapēnā se tamaitiiti aʻoaʻoina.
examples.en: A well-raised child doesn't act like that.

title: Weddings
summary: Name the people, things and events of a Samoan wedding. You'll also ask about the service and the gifts.

notes.point: Many wedding words are built with faʻaipoipo (marry): the bride is the teine faʻaipoipo, the groom the tama faʻaipoipo, the wedding the faʻaipoipoga.
uōsili (from the English) is the best man or bridesmaid; say tama or teine to tell them apart.

title: Funerals
summary: Know the words for the events of a Samoan funeral, from the announcement to the burial. You'll also ask when someone died and when the funeral is.

notes.point: Samoan has respect words for dying: tuʻumālō for a high chief, usufono for an orator, maliu as the polite word, and oti for the plain one.

examples.en: When did he die? (a high chief)

title: Medicinal plants
summary: Ask the name and use of a medicinal plant and say how often to take a medicine or a massage. You'll also follow simple steps for making Samoan medicine.

notes.point: Ask what a plant is with ʻo ā lāʻau, and what it's for with ʻo le ā le aogā o.

examples.sm: ʻO le ā le aogā o le launonu?
examples.en: What's the noni leaf used for?

notes.point: Say how often with faʻa- before the number: faʻatasi (once), faʻalua (twice). Ask with faʻafia (how many times).

examples.en: How many times a day do you take it?

examples.en: Once in the morning, once in the afternoon.

notes.point: Directions for making medicine are commands joined with ona ... loa lea (then).

examples.en: Let it cool, then drink it.

phrases.en: How many times a day is the massage?

culture: A taulāsea is a healer who treats illnesses linked to spirits; fofō is the general word for a healer, some for sprains and breaks, some for children. Healers use leaves and plants, often with medicines passed down in a family, and you may be offered a Samoan massage.

title: Samoan cricket
summary: Know the words for kirikiti, Samoa's own cricket, and shout the lines you'll hear on the field. You'll also know how Samoan rules differ from English cricket.

notes.point: Calls on the field are short commands.

culture: Kirikiti is a national sport, with a national league once a year. Villages have their own pitches and often their own rules; a ball hit over the boundary in the air scores 2, and one that rolls over scores 1.
sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 46

title: Everyday expressions
summary: Use a few casual Samoan expressions friends say to each other. You'll also recognize the k-style of everyday speech.

notes.point: In casual talk many people say k for t and g for n. You'll hear kālofa for tālofa and faʻafekai for faʻafetai.

sources: Gagana Samoa mo Pisikoa (Peace Corps, 1991), Lesson 48

title: Guessing Games: ʻO le ā le mea?
summary: A guessing game played with words you already know. One player thinks of a thing, gives short clues, and the others guess with ʻO le ...? until someone names it.

notes.point: The player who has a thing in mind opens the round by asking ʻO le ā le mea?, a question that asks for the name of the thing. Everyone else guesses by saying ʻO le and a noun with a question in the voice.
Answer each guess with ʻIoe (yes) or Leai (no). After a no, give a clue: E followed by a describing word.
A sharper guess adds the describing word after the noun, never before it.
In a spelling round, where the answer is spelled out letter by letter, the ʻokina counts as a letter of its own, just like p or a.

examples.en: flying fox (four letters: p, e, ʻ, a)

lines.sm: E uliuli. ʻO le ā le mea?
lines.en: It's black. What is the thing?

practice.q: Which means 'to sleep' for more than one person?

culture: Many of the words here name things you can see in a village: the fala (sleeping mat), the taʻinamu (mosquito net), the paopao (small canoe) and the lali (wooden drum). Playing the game with objects in the room or along the road is a quick way to practise their names out loud.

title: Review: The Basics Again
summary: A check on the first things you learned: taking and bringing, this and that, talking about more than one, greetings, putting things on or in, and the seven days of the week.

notes.point: Pick the verb by direction. ʻAumai moves a thing toward you, the speaker; ʻave moves it away from you. Before a person's name, 'to' is iā (also written ʻiā).
This and that depend on distance: lenei for something by the speaker, lenā for something by the listener, lelā for something away from you both.
To talk about more than one, leave le out. In most cases the noun itself keeps its form.
A basic greeting runs in four steps: say Tālofa, ask after the other person with ʻO ā mai ʻoe?, hear Manuia faʻafetai (fine, thanks) in reply, and say Tōfā when you leave.

examples.sm: Manuia lava faʻafetai. ʻAe ā ʻoe?

notes.point: Each day name begins with Aso (day). Monday is Aso Gafua, Tuesday is Aso Lua, then come Aso Lulu, Aso Tofi and Aso Faraile for Wednesday to Friday, with Aso Toʻonaʻi for Saturday and Aso Sā for Sunday. Use i le in front for 'on' or 'by' a day.

examples.sm: E te faigāluega i le Aso Toʻonaʻi?

notes.point: To say where something goes, use tuʻu, then the thing, then i luga o (on top of) or i totonu o (inside) and the place.

examples.sm: Tuʻu le uati i luga o le laulau.
examples.en: Put the watch on the table.

examples.sm: Tuʻu le peni i totonu o le ʻato.
examples.en: Put the pen in the bag.

lines.sm: Tālofa Ioane. ʻO ā mai ʻoe?
Manuia lava. ʻAumai le sāmala, faʻamolemole.
lines.en: Very well. Bring the hammer, please.

lines.sm: Faʻafetai. ʻAve le pakete ʻiā Pita.
lines.en: Thanks. Take the bucket to Pita.

lines.sm: ʻOu te alu ʻi le faleʻoloa. Tōfā.
lines.en: I'm going to the shop. Bye.
